lessons.title: Knowing what is in the water
lessons.html:
Why stock control matters

You cannot see fish the way you can count cattle in a kraal. Yet every decision on a fish farm, from how much feed to order to when to harvest and what to sell, depends on knowing how many fish you have and how big they are. Stock control is the system of records and sampling that gives you those numbers.

Core stock figures per unit

  • Number of fish stocked, less mortalities, less fish moved out.
  • Average weight from regular sample weighing.
  • Biomass = number of fish x average weight. This drives the feed ration.
  • Stocking density = biomass per cubic metre (tanks) or per hectare or square metre (ponds).

Sample weighing

  1. Sample at a regular interval set by the manager, often every two to four weeks.
  2. Stop feeding before sampling as the procedure says.
  3. Catch a random, representative sample; do not just scoop the fish that come to the surface first, as these are often the biggest.
  4. Weigh the fish in a tared bucket of water and count them.
  5. Calculate average weight and record the spread of sizes.
  6. Return fish quickly and gently.

Mortality records

Count and record dead fish every day per unit. Unrecorded mortalities make the stock figure too high, so feed is overestimated and wasted. Escapes and predation by birds also reduce stock, which is why counts at harvest often differ from the book figure.

Movements

Every transfer between units, sale, or restocking must be recorded with date, number, total weight and source and destination unit. A batch or cohort number lets you trace each group of fish from hatchery to harvest.

lessons.title: Using stock records to manage the farm
lessons.html:
From numbers to decisions

Good stock records turn into practical management information.

Feed conversion ratio (FCR)

FCR = feed given / weight gained. For example, if a unit gained 1 000 kg of fish and was fed 1 500 kg of feed, the FCR is 1.5. A rising FCR means feed is being wasted, fish are stressed or sick, or the stock figure is wrong. Because feed is the largest cost, FCR is one of the most watched numbers on the farm.

Growth and survival

  • Growth rate: change in average weight per day or per week between samples.
  • Survival: fish alive now as a percentage of fish stocked.

Compare these between units, seasons and fingerling suppliers to find what works.

Harvest planning

Knowing biomass and growth rate lets you forecast when units will reach market size and how much fish you will have each month. Buyers and processors need reliable supply, so forecasts must be honest.

Stock reconciliation

At harvest compare actual numbers and weight with the book figures. A large difference points to unrecorded deaths, theft, escapes, predators or poor sampling. Investigate and correct the system.

Consumables stock

Stock control also covers feed, chemicals, nets and spare parts. Keep a stock card for each item with receipts, issues and balance. Check physical stock against the cards regularly. Use first-in, first-out for feed, and watch expiry dates on feed, remedies and test kits.

RecordUsed for
Daily mortalitiesAccurate numbers, early disease warning
Sample weightsBiomass, feed ration, growth rate
Feed issuedFCR, feed ordering, cost control
Movements and salesTraceability, reconciliation

Key points

  • Biomass = number of fish x average weight.
  • Take random, representative samples at regular intervals.
  • Record every death, transfer and sale per unit.
  • FCR = feed given / weight gained; a rising FCR needs investigating.
  • Reconcile book stock with actual harvest figures.
